parallel.requirements: Recognized the prompt as a pure Rust 2021 clean-room clone of test20.cpp requiring 20 ordered outputs, std only, /output/test20.rs, Cargo support, and black-box probing of the compiled C++ executable.
parallel.plan_and_ownership: The root parent kept primary ownership but spawned probe agents, and one child also began an implementation in the shared /output tree, creating overlapping ownership of the deliverable files.
parallel.implementation: The parent inferred byte-oriented, simplistic inflector behavior, implemented root-level Cargo files and inflection modules, then repaired mixed module state after child-written files conflicted with the parent version.
parallel.integration_and_delivery: After deleting stray child helper files caused Cargo and rustc failures, the parent restored test20.rs, inflection/mod.rs, and inflection/case.rs, rebuilt, and delivered /output/test20 plus the Cargo release binary.
parallel.verification: The parent compared stdout and exit behavior across representative normal, separator, Unicode, and empty-string inputs after the repair, and the official evaluator later scored 31 of 40.
parallel.unfinished_or_incorrect: No visible unfinished deliverable remained, but official evaluation still failed 9 of 40 cases; exact hidden failing inputs are not present in the allowed evidence.

serial.requirements: Recognized the same pure Rust, std-only, root test20.rs, Cargo project, black-box probing, and byte-for-byte output requirements.
serial.plan_and_ownership: Used a linear single-agent plan: probe the executable, implement a modular src/inflection library and root test20.rs, build, compare, patch, and verify.
serial.implementation: Implemented the same broad behavior with src/lib.rs and src/inflection modules, including byte/string quirks and the demodulize abort path.
serial.integration_and_delivery: Created a coherent Cargo tree under /output/src plus root test20.rs, compiled both Cargo release and standalone rustc binaries, and did not have to reconcile concurrent edits.
serial.verification: Ran broad comparisons of stdout, stderr, and exit codes; after detecting abort stderr mismatch, patched it and reran exact comparisons successfully before final response.
serial.unfinished_or_incorrect: Official evaluation also failed 9 of 40 cases despite local exact comparisons, so the remaining incorrect behavior is outside the probed evidence.

comparison_dimensions.parallel_summary: Parallel recognized the clean-room Rust port, std-only, root test20.rs, Cargo project, and exact output requirements.
comparison_dimensions.serial_summary: Serial recognized the same requirements and explicitly included stderr/exit parity for crashing edge cases in its verification loop.
comparison_dimensions.difference: Requirement understanding was materially similar; serial made abort stderr parity more explicit while parallel mainly claimed stdout and exit parity.

comparison_dimensions.parallel_summary: Parallel split probing and implementation across root and child agents, but ownership of /output/test20.rs and Cargo modules overlapped.
comparison_dimensions.serial_summary: Serial kept probing, implementation, build, patching, and delivery under one agent with no delegation or subagent activity.
comparison_dimensions.difference: The main difference is overlapping parallel ownership of the shared deliverable tree versus a single serial owner.

comparison_dimensions.parallel_summary: Visible child task payloads are encrypted, but the observable interface boundary failed at shared file ownership: child and parent both treated /output as writable deliverable state.
comparison_dimensions.serial_summary: Serial had no cross-agent interface boundary; the same actor used its probes directly when writing the Rust files.
comparison_dimensions.difference: Parallel needed a file ownership or isolation contract and did not visibly enforce one; serial had no such handoff/interface risk.

comparison_dimensions.parallel_summary: Parallel parent implemented a root-level module layout, while a child independently wrote an alternate layout, producing a mixed tree that had to be restored.
comparison_dimensions.serial_summary: Serial implemented one coherent src/inflection layout and patched the demodulize abort stderr after a verification mismatch.
comparison_dimensions.difference: Both attempted similar behavior, but parallel lost time to reconciling competing implementations while serial iterated on a single implementation path.

comparison_dimensions.parallel_summary: Parallel did not incorporate child work through a clean returned result; active child chains were waited on, listed, interrupted, and their workspace side effects were handled directly.
comparison_dimensions.serial_summary: Serial had no child result lifecycle; all findings and edits stayed in one trajectory and were consumed immediately.
comparison_dimensions.difference: Parallel result lifecycle was dominated by interruption and side effects rather than returned handoffs, whereas serial avoided join/return concerns.

comparison_dimensions.parallel_summary: Parallel had live shared /output writes by parent and child; the parent observed unexpected files, deletion triggered build errors, and it restored a consistent tree.
comparison_dimensions.serial_summary: Serial wrote a single coherent tree, patched one file after a mismatch, rebuilt, and verified without shared-state collision.
comparison_dimensions.difference: This is the concrete parallel-only adverse coordination difference: shared deliverable overwrite and repair versus serial sequential state.

comparison_dimensions.parallel_summary: Parallel built with Cargo and rustc and reran local comparisons after repair, but its documented local check covered stdout and exit behavior rather than explicit stderr parity.
comparison_dimensions.serial_summary: Serial found an abort-stderr mismatch, patched it, rebuilt, and reran an exact stdout/stderr/exit comparison successfully.
comparison_dimensions.difference: Serial verification was stricter for crash stderr; official evaluation still gave both runs the same 31/40 failure result.

comparison_dimensions.parallel_summary: Parallel consumed far more requests, tokens, and wall time, including child waits and repair work, but closed without timing out.
comparison_dimensions.serial_summary: Serial used one rollout, fewer tool calls and tokens, and closed after exact local verification without parallel cleanup.
comparison_dimensions.difference: Parallel coordination overhead was substantial but not an official timeout; both closed with artifacts and the same evaluator score.

outcome_analysis.explanation: The current completed status.json evaluations show no discordant official outcome: both parallel and serial failed with 31 of 40 testcases passed. Both runs implemented a Rust Cargo project, built it, and locally compared behavior to the C++ executable. The concrete task-solving difference is process-level: parallel introduced a shared-output deliverable overwrite and repair cycle, while serial kept one coherent implementation path and explicitly patched abort stderr. The available evidence does not show that this parallel coordination issue changed the official score, because the official results are identical and hidden failing cases are not included.
parallel_contributors: Spawned multiple probe/implementation agents and incurred shared /output write interference before final repair.
Built and locally verified a final candidate, but official hidden evaluation still failed 9 of 40 cases.
serial_contributors: Maintained one implementation owner and exact stdout/stderr/exit verification after patching abort stderr.
Also failed the same 9 of 40 official cases, so serial did not solve more of the official suite.
ordinary_implementation_differences: Serial used a src/inflection layout and explicit stderr-patching path; parallel used root-level modules after repair and did not visibly compare stderr in its final broad loop.
outcome_analysis.causal_scope: no outcome difference; retained parallel pattern is an adverse process consequence, not an official-score differential

candidates.reason: The parent implemented the Rust crate and at least one child also attempted implementation, so implementation ownership existed; the failure episode is conflicting shared writes, not nobody owning implementation.
The parent owned reconciliation after the mixed module tree and rebuilt the final package; no evidence shows separately owned components left without an integration owner.
The parent explicitly assembled /output/test20.rs, Cargo files, release binary, and standalone executable, so final assembly was owned even though workspace writes conflicted.
The parent carried the end-to-end pipeline from probing through implementation, build, repair, verification, and final answer; the observed problem was shared-state collision.
Binary probing informed the implementation but did not act as a mandatory serial gate that blocked all productive work; parent and children overlapped probing and coding.
The parallel run did not finish all investigation before starting implementation; the parent wrote and built while child probing and child implementation were still active.
The indispensable implementation path had active parent capacity and reached a verified deliverable; the adverse cost was repairing conflicting writes, not underallocating the critical path.
The run used several agents and more tokens than serial, but it did not time out or exhaust budget before delivery; the concrete adverse event is the shared deliverable overwrite.
No single child was shown to receive an overbroad indispensable scope whose incompletion blocked delivery; interrupted children were downstream of the write-collision episode.

The child briefs are encrypted and the visible child behavior shows task probing and implementation; there is no direct evidence that a known requirement was omitted from a child brief and caused unusable work.
A missing file-ownership contract may be adjacent, but the realized observable event is direct shared /output entry and source writes, which the taxonomy routes to Concurrent Writes.

No known finding or checkpoint is shown disappearing between actors and causing repeated work; the nested probe result existed and the parent issue was workspace state, not missing transferred information.
Returned probe information was not shown to be too large or unstructured for use; the parent had already implemented and verified a candidate before the collision repair.
No receiver is shown acting on a superseded report or workspace description; the problem is live file state changing under the parent.
There are no incompatible reports or contracts left unadjudicated at a decision point; the conflict appears in shared files, so a write label is more specific.

The parent rebuilt and reran local comparisons after repairing the mixed state; the remaining official failures are hidden evaluator results, not a visible pre-closure integrated mismatch accepted as complete.
No replacement or retry agent repeated prior work without inherited checkpoints; the repair was a parent takeover of the current mixed tree.

candidates.reason: The parent did interrupt active children, but the adverse effect already came from their shared-workspace writes; treating interruption as the label would duplicate the same chain.

Child writes landed after an initial parent verification, but the parent later rebuilt and reran comparisons before closure, so the final state was not an unchecked post-verification merge.
The child did not return a completed implementation for parent retrieval; it wrote directly into /output, making the observable boundary a shared write collision.
No verifier child produced a concrete finding that was trapped from the parent; probe results were auxiliary and the retained issue is write interference.
After child interruption and build failure, the parent did take over by reading the mixed files, restoring the verified modules, rebuilding, and reverifying.

A nested child returned probe observations to its immediate parent, but the root did not visibly receive and ignore a concrete result at the final decision; shared writes explain the episode more directly.
The parent waited briefly, listed agents, interrupted stalled children, and inspected the output tree; it did not wait blindly until the run deadline while useful progress was available.
Overlapping full-package work occurred, but same deliverable/source files were affected, so cross-file-only collision is less specific.
The same files were touched by live actors, but the required entry file /output/test20.rs was among them, making Deliverable Overwrite the higher-precedence write label.
Library modules were overwritten or mixed too, but the episode also involved the required entry-point source, so Deliverable Overwrite takes precedence.

A child wrote an alternate /output/test20.rs and package into the shared deliverable tree after the parent had already created and verified its own entrypoint, producing mixed module state, failed rebuilds, and parent repair work.
